walkthrough:
Sort By How The Phenotype Looks**
Think of discontinuous as either-or and continuous as a sliding scale. Discontinuous traits fall into discrete categories with no intermediates, like albino or not albino, blood group A, B, AB or O. Continuous traits show a full range of intermediates, like human height from very short to very tall with every value in between.

Link Pattern To Number Of Genes**
The pattern comes from the genetics. Discontinuous variation is usually monogenic - one or a few genes control the phenotype. Continuous variation is polygenic - several genes at different loci all contribute to the same trait. That is why height or grain yield can vary so smoothly.

Add In Size Of Allelic Effect**
In discontinuous variation, different alleles at the single locus have a large effect, so genotype switches phenotype clearly. Different genes also have different effects. In continuous variation, different alleles at each locus have only a small, additive effect, so you need many of them together to shift the phenotype noticeably.

Bring In The Environment**
This is a key difference. Discontinuous phenotypes have little or no environmental contribution - your ABO group or albinism is fixed by genotype. Continuous phenotypes are strongly influenced by environment as well as genes - height is affected by nutrition, plant mass by water, light and minerals. That environmental blurring helps create the smooth range.

Use Correct Language And Named Examples**
Describe discontinuous as qualitative and continuous as quantitative. Qualitative means descriptive categories. Quantitative means measurable with numbers. Always pair each side with a named example: discontinuous e.g. albinism, sickle cell anaemia, haemophilia, Huntington's disease; continuous e.g. height, body mass.

Final answer: Discontinuous: controlled by one / few genes, qualitative, discrete categories with no intermediates, different alleles have large effect, little / no environmental influence, e.g. albinism / sickle cell anaemia / haemophilia. Continuous: controlled by many genes (polygenic), quantitative, range of intermediates, different alleles have small additive effects, strong environmental influence, e.g. height / body mass.

walkthrough:
The Core Cycle Of Selective Breeding**
Humans replace natural selection. Choose parent plants showing good features such as large grains, high yield or disease resistance. Breed these selected parents together, select the best offspring and repeat for many generations. Favourable alleles increase in frequency and yield rises.

Protecting Yield With Disease Resistance**
A lot of potential yield is lost to pathogens. Breeders cross high-yielding varieties with wild relatives carrying resistance alleles, then backcross to keep yield plus resistance. Less infection means more healthy leaf for photosynthesis and more grain filled.

Dwarf Varieties Put Energy Into Grain**
Modern wheat and maize are short-stemmed dwarfs. They carry mutant alleles that reduce gibberellin synthesis, so stems elongate less. Less photosynthate is spent on tall stems and more is partitioned to grain. Short, sturdy stems are also less likely to be knocked over by wind and rain, known as lodging, so less crop is lost.

Inbreeding For Uniformity Then Hybrid Vigour For Yield**
Repeated self-pollination or crossing close relatives (inbreeding) makes lines homozygous and uniform. That is useful because all plants are standard height and cobs / ears are ready to harvest at the same time, ideal for machines. Crossing two different inbred lines (hybridisation) then produces heterozygous offspring that show hybrid vigour - faster growth, larger size and higher grain yield than either parent.

Final answer: Select parents with desirable features and cross-breed them, repeated over many generations. Introduce disease resistance alleles to reduce loss. Select dwarf varieties with mutant gibberellin synthesis alleles, so more assimilates to grain and less lodging. Inbreeding gives uniformity e.g. same height / simultaneous ripening for harvest. Hybridisation of inbred lines gives hybrid vigour and increased yield.
